newsitem.title: USA: Prosecutors winding up case against Ariz. governor.
newsitem.headline: Prosecutors winding up case against Ariz. governor.

text.p: Assistant U.S. Attorney George Cardona described Arizona Governor Fife Symington Wednesday as a liar who knew what he was doing when he defrauded lenders in his days as a developer.
In closing arguments for the prosecution, jury members were urged to use their common sense to disregard Symington's testimony on allegations of fraud, attempted extortion and perjury.

Cardona asserted Symington engaged in a conscious pattern of deceit when it came to revealing his financial picture in his dealings with lenders in the turbulent real estate market of the mid-1980s to early 1990s.
"Mr. Symington told lenders what they wanted to hear," Cordona told the jury, adding that Symington's six days on the witness stand were spent telling the jury what he felt it needed to hear.

By calling Symington's credibility into question, the government all but wrapped up its three-month case with an all-out offensive in trying to prove he committed 21 counts of fraud, attempted extortion and perjury.

He had faced another felony count, but it was dismissed late Tuesday by U.S. Judge Roger Strand because he felt it had not been proved Mercantile Bank of Baltimore was defrauded when it issued Symington a $300,000 letter of credit.
If convicted on even a single count, the 51-year-old Republican would be ousted from the office he has held since 1991. He also could get a prison term.
During Wednesday's remarks, Cardona described Symington as a knowledgeable, Harvard-educated man who lied for a purpose, not out of ignorance as he had claimed.
He said Symington was at fault, not the banks who did not ask about information contained on his financial statements nor the accountants who did not catch his errors.
He told the jury that Symington could be excused for a few mistakes on the statements submitted to lenders during his days as a developer, but not for "20, 30, 40 falsehoods."

The prosecutor said that the government had proved beyond a reasonable doubt that Symington had to have known that the information he was giving lenders was false, saying he negotiated for the loans and signed the documents.
Cardona added that the evidence proved Symington took considerable "time and trouble" to track what statements he gave to lenders, who entrusted him with millions of dollars.

Additionally, Cardona asked the jury to believe the notes from two pension fund advisers which revealed threats made by Symington to try to extort concessions from pension funds that loaned him $10 million for a downtown Phoenix office-retail project. Symington said there was no such threat.
He also told jurors that Symington lied during bankruptcy proceedings as a creditor's attorney pressed him about his finances. He filed for Chapter 7 in September 1995.
The defence is expected to present closing arguments Thursday. The jury could get the case late Thursday.
